newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Russia's Lebed relishes limelight, praises NATO.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed relishes limelight, praises NATO.

text.p: Russian security chief Alexander Lebed, relishing his debut on the world political stage, emerged from NATO's military nerve centre on Tuesday praising the alliance and pledging closer co-operation.

Lebed, a reserve general who makes no secret of his ambition one day to succeed Boris Yeltsin as president, described the command centre as an "efficient, well-tuned military machine". He said he was pleased with his first Western visit.
Lebed earlier inspected an honour guard of allied soldiers with Supreme Allied Commander Europe, U.S. General George Joulwan, before touring SHAPE headquarters.
The sprawling military headquarters would have played a major part in directing any military operations against the now disbanded Warsaw Pact which Lebed served through most of his career.
"We spoke as two soldiers," Lebed said after emerging into the sunshine from the central control building known as Live Oak. "We talked as two paratroopers."
"For paratroopers there are no impossible tasks," he said, his heavy face breaking into a broad smile.

Lebed's visit, his first venture onto western soil three months after his rise to prominence in presidential elections, has been watched closely by Western officials eager to get the measure of the political newcomer. Interest has been made keener by uncertainty over Yeltsin's approaching heart surgery.

The former 14th Army commander has struck a markedly moderate tone, in contrast to past outspoken attacks on NATO for its plans to expand eastwards. He has also criticised the Partnership for Peace (PfP) agreement establishing loose mlitary links with east European countries and Russia.
PfP, he said recently, had become little more than an ante- room for former Warsaw Pact allies of Moscow to enter NATO.
But standing in front of Live Oak, a flimsy-looking two- storey building atop an enormous underground complex, he changed his assessment.
"I concluded the country I have the honour to represent has by no means exploited fully the opportunities offered by PfP.
"I am sure that in the near future, we will be able to organise serious co-operation," he said. Joulwan nodded accord.
Lebed also said Russia was ready to contribute troops to any "follow-on" contingent in Bosnia after the mission of the current NATO-led IFOR peacekeeping force ends in December.
"We will play a serious part," he said.
Russia currently has almost 2,000 troops in Bosnia and has an IFOR liaison officer working alongside Joulwan in Mons.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana has proposed an exchange of permanent liaison officers between Moscow and the alliance to quell lingering Russian suspicions.

In Budapest, a senior NATO military official said on Tuesday the alliance would not slow down its eastward expansion despite Lebed's appeal to it to "take stock, take stock and take stock again." Klaus Naumann, chairman of the alliance's military committee, said the expansion would pose no threat to Moscow.
NATO intends to invite countries to open entry talks next yar, with Poland, Hungary and the Czech republc seen as the most likely candidates.
Lebed began his visit to Mons by signing Joulwan's visitor's book and declaring: "The planet earth needs reason and intelligence and not wars. Let it be so."
Joulwan intoned: "Together, we can make it happen".

The public declarations of Lebed's visit have been encouraging to Western diplomats. Most have been impressed by the moderation of the man who only recently described NATO as acting like a drunken hooligan in a kindergarten.
But they might well be left wondering what has happened to the more flamboyant and hostile Lebed and whether, perhaps, they might hear from him again as the political fray in Moscow intensifies.
